title: A Different Kind of Pilot: Deposition Simulator Emerges as a Training Tool for Big Law Associates
author: Jon Campisi

dom.t: AI simulation: Practice substitutes remain unvalidated

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts the need to reconstruct associate apprenticeship and provides a concrete implementation example: realistic deposition simulations that supplement existing training, give juniors experience they may not receive on live matters, and incorporate feedback. It strengthens the cluster’s proposed response, though it offers no independent or quantitative evidence of long-term learning outcomes.
qs: "It is really a supplement [to] training programs that we are already doing to give associates experience that they would not otherwise have," she said.
Depositions are a core part of litigation, Daves said, and oftentimes in real life young associates are not the ones taking the actual depositions.

st.t: AI simulation: Practice substitutes remain unvalidated
st.an: The source supports AI simulation as a supplemental, low-consequence way to provide deposition practice within broader firm training, while preserving the need for human judgment. Its evidence is limited to adoption, participant reactions and vendor plans rather than measured improvements in advocacy, aligning with the cluster’s conclusion that practice substitution remains unvalidated.

kp.k: Four firms adopt AI role-playing for deposition training
kp.d: The June 22, 2026 American Lawyer feature reports adoption of DepoSim at Orrick, Taft, Brownstein and Littler. Developed by AltaClaro with Verbit, it simulates witnesses, opposing counsel and court reporters for early-career training and experienced-lawyer refreshers. Its claimed first-of-kind status is attributed to its makers, rather than established through comparative evidence.
qs: DepoSim was developed through a partnership between legal training provider AltaClaro and legal transcription provider Verbit. The makers consider the training simulator to be the first of its kind in the legal market.

Law firms including Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe, Taft Stettinius & Hollister, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck and Littler Mendelson have all incorporated an AI-powered deposition simulator for associate training.

kp.k: Orrick reports greater peer engagement through AI training
kp.d: Orrick litigation training council leader Matthew LaBrie says the firm's implementation unexpectedly increased interaction and peer-to-peer engagement, contrasting favorably with theoretical instruction and video lectures. Kelly Cullen places adoption within an earlier onboarding reform that removed revenue-generating requirements for associates' first six months to prioritize practical team experience and training; the article does not attribute that reform to AI.
qs: One of the things that surprised me most about how we've implemented [DepoSim] is that using AI has actually caused greater interaction and greater peer-to-peer engagement,

Kelly Cullen, an Orrick lawyer who heads up associate development and training, said, a few years back, the firm decided to put a greater emphasis on onboarding junior lawyers, eliminating their revenue-generating requirements for the first six months of employment in order to enable them to gain practical experience working on teams and focusing more heavily on training.

kp.k: Taft combines consistent training with individualized practice
kp.d: Taft's Chasity Thompson Osborn describes the simulator as supporting consistent foundational training while allowing customization for different skill levels. Chief client and innovation officer Lyndsay Capeder says adoption reflected an established AltaClaro relationship and assessment of expected professional-development impact, rather than acquiring AI tools for their own sake.
qs: This gives them the opportunity to customize the experience that they have and at the various skill levels that they have,

Taft, she said, is not "in the business of just running around and collecting AI tools just for the sake of collecting AI tools," but rather the firm takes the time to evaluate which tools are expected to have the most meaningful impact on lawyers and their professional development.

kp.k: Simulation offers practice without exposing clients to inexperience
kp.d: Taft litigation co-chair Lynn Rowe Larsen describes an opportunity for younger litigators to adjust their approach during a simulated deposition without practicing on a client's live matter. She also presents the tool as a refresher for experienced attorneys whose practices have not recently involved depositions.
qs: They can adjust what they're doing throughout the course of a deposition,
And sometimes clients don't really want you to practice on their legal matter in a live deposition.

You can maybe use it for an hour or so and kind of get back into the habit and the rhythm of the evidentiary objections of the process of taking a deposition if maybe you haven't had any in your practice in a while,

kp.k: Littler uses simulation to supplement scarce junior deposition experience
kp.d: Littler's Jeanine Conley Daves says junior associates often do not take their own depositions until they are mid-year associates. She presents DepoSim as a supplement to existing training that converts subject expertise into practice, helps lawyers tailor questioning to witness demeanor, and provides otherwise unavailable experience and feedback.
qs: Daves said the concept behind DepoSim is great because it prepares lawyers, especially junior level associates, on how to tailor their questioning style to match witness demeanor.
It is really a supplement [to] training programs that we are already doing to give associates experience that they would not otherwise have,
These junior lawyers may not even get to actually take depositions on their own until they're mid-year associates.

kp.k: Brownstein reports positive feedback from nine initial testers
kp.d: Chief talent officer Margaux Trammell says Brownstein initially tested DepoSim with three junior associates, three mid-to-senior associates and three partners, receiving uniformly high feedback. Participants reportedly valued practicing aloud without consequences, confidence building, constructive performance feedback and comparisons with earlier sessions. These are reported participant reactions, not measured improvements in litigation performance. Adoption fits the firm's three-year strategic plan for increased AI use.
qs: She said the firm initially tested DepoSim with three junior associates, three mid-to-senior associates and three partners, some younger and others more senior.
This one was unanimously received [with] a very high mark,
I can speak out loud, and if I fail, it's totally OK because there are no consequences,
The lawyers, she added, also appreciate the fact that DepoSim can offer constructive feedback on performance, and compare that with prior sessions.

kp.k: Firm collaboration shaped the simulator before development
kp.d: AltaClaro founder and CEO Abdi Shayesteh credits pre-build design feedback from Cullen and Orrick colleagues. He contrasts collaborative early adopters with firms preferring to wait until others resolve glitches. His statement that AltaClaro serves over 100 Am Law 200 firms concerns the company's broader client base, not a reported DepoSim adoption count.
qs: We did the heavy lifting, but they gave us such good feedback before we even built it,
We service over 100 Am Law 200 firms, and not every firm is innovative like this,
Some firms are like, 'yeah, let others go first, work out the glitches, and then I'll buy it.'

kp.k: Vendor claims simulation can reduce traditional training costs
kp.d: AltaClaro leaders argue that DepoSim can save training costs relative to hiring actors for one-time deposition exercises or sending associates to costly off-site programs. The feature provides no quantified savings or cost comparison.
qs: AltaClaro leaders said DepoSim can actually help firms save costs on training, since traditionally law firms have incurred substantial expenses in hiring actors for one-time deposition role-playing or sending associates to often costly off-site training programs.

kp.k: Planned expansion emphasizes enduring human judgment skills
kp.d: Shayesteh argues that lawyers will continue to need human judgment and thinking on their feet despite AI taking over some industry activities. AltaClaro proposes extending simulations beyond depositions into cross-examination, opening and closing statements, oral argument, client interviews and negotiation, across additional practice areas. These are future plans rather than reported deployed capabilities.
qs: While AI is taking over certain aspects of the legal industry, lawyers will still always need to involve their human skills "for the thinking on your feet, the judgment skills," he said.

In the future, the company plans to expand the platform to include additional simulations across commercial litigation, employment law, intellectual property, expert witness depositions, trial practice, oral arguments, client interviews and negotiation scenarios.

kp.k: Vendor summary adds rollout dates and training philosophy
kp.d: The secondary AltaClaro page, published on 22 June 2026, frames the feature as supporting the vendor's belief in low-stakes practice before real client work. Its linked announcements date Brownstein's launch to 4 June 2026, Taft's firmwide launch to 17 March 2026 and Littler's firmwide launch to 20 May 2026. This framing and dating come from the vendor summary, distinct from the licensed feature.
qs: Through interviews with partners, professional development leaders, and innovation executives, the article captures something we have believed from the start: that the future of legal training depends on giving lawyers a place to practice, fail, and grow before the stakes are real.
The page also links three AltaClaro launch announcements — Brownstein (4 June 2026), Taft firmwide (17 March 2026) and Littler firmwide (20 May 2026) — which date the individual rollouts.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The feature reports current adoption of AI simulation for litigation training; interviewed lawyers describe more interactive practice, earlier access to deposition experience, adaptable training and skill reinforcement. AltaClaro predicts cost savings and broader simulation offerings.
pts.d: Jon Campisi reports that Orrick, Taft, Brownstein and Littler have incorporated DepoSim, developed by AltaClaro with Verbit, into associate training. The simulator uses AI role-playing witnesses, opposing counsel and court reporters; this is training support, not replacement of lawyers in live proceedings. Orrick partner Matthew LaBrie says the firm's implementation increased peer interaction and engagement, contrary to his expectations, and offers a more engaging alternative to theoretical or video-based instruction. Taft's Chasity Thompson Osborn says users can customize practice to their skill levels. Taft partner Lynn Rowe Larsen says lawyers can adjust their approach during simulated depositions and experienced lawyers can refresh deposition skills without practicing on a client's live matter. Littler's Jeanine Conley Daves says the simulator supplements existing training by allowing juniors to conduct depositions, adapt questioning to different witness personalities, receive feedback and build confidence before they would ordinarily lead real depositions. Brownstein's Margaux Trammell describes realistic, interactive practice, consequence-free opportunities to fail, and performance feedback that can be compared with prior sessions. AltaClaro's leaders claim potential training-cost savings relative to hiring actors or sending associates to off-site programs. CEO Abdi Shayesteh predicts expansion into other interpersonal legal tasks while asserting an enduring need for human judgment and thinking on one's feet. The makers' first-of-its-kind positioning and AltaClaro's secondary-page claim about the future of legal training are vendor claims, distinct from the firms' implementation accounts.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is named-firm adoption, practitioner experience and qualitative feedback, including a nine-lawyer Brownstein pilot; savings and future expansion are supported by vendor reasoning and plans rather than measured outcomes.
pts.d: Campisi draws on interviews with litigation partners, professional-development leaders and innovation executives at the four adopting firms. LaBrie's engagement claim is an observation about Orrick's own implementation. Osborn, Larsen and Daves describe uses and perceived benefits within their firms, rather than controlled comparisons. Trammell reports that Brownstein tested the simulator with three junior associates, three mid-to-senior associates and three partners, with uniformly positive reception; no numerical ratings or measured skill gains are supplied. User feedback supports reported confidence-building potential and appreciation of interactivity and performance feedback. AltaClaro points to collaborative design with Orrick and positive client feedback as validation. Shayesteh's statement that AltaClaro serves more than 100 Am Law 200 firms establishes the vendor's broader customer context, not DepoSim's adoption count. The cost-saving claim rests on comparison with the expenses of actors and off-site training, without quantified costs or savings. The article supplies no benchmark, controlled training study, longitudinal performance assessment or client-outcome data. First-of-its-kind status is presented as the makers' view. The secondary page is AltaClaro's own selected summary and promotional framing, not an additional independent evaluation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reported benefits concern early implementations by June 2026; wider applications and savings are prospective and unquantified, while enduring human judgment is an explicit long-term prediction.
pts.d: The feature is dated June 22, 2026. The supplied secondary material dates linked rollout announcements to March 17, 2026 for Taft firmwide, May 20, 2026 for Littler firmwide and June 4, 2026 for Brownstein; it provides no specific Orrick rollout date. Statements about current benefits refer to experience to that point, and LaBrie specifically conditions increased peer engagement on how Orrick implemented the tool. Daves describes supplementation of an already robust training program rather than wholesale replacement. Larsen suggests an experienced lawyer might use the tool for about an hour to regain familiarity after a period without depositions. Orrick's removal of revenue-generating requirements for associates' first six months began a few years earlier and is background training policy, not an identified effect of DepoSim. Brownstein places adoption within its three-year strategic plan. Shayesteh acknowledges uneven adoption, with some firms waiting for others to resolve glitches. Future simulations have no delivery dates: the company plans commercial litigation, employment, intellectual property, expert depositions, trial practice, oral argument, client interviews and negotiation, and Shayesteh identifies cross-examination and opening and closing statements as likely additions. Potential cost savings are not assigned a timeframe or magnitude. His claim that human judgment will always remain necessary is a prediction, not an observed long-run result.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is early-career litigators at large law firms, with additional benefits claimed for experienced lawyers, training teams and firms' training budgets; clients are indirectly affected through reduced reliance on live matters for practice.
pts.d: Junior associates are the main intended users: simulation offers speaking practice, adaptable witness interactions, feedback and opportunities to lead a deposition before such opportunities arise in client work. Mid-level and senior associates and partners can refresh or reinforce skills; Brownstein's pilot included all three seniority groups. Litigation-training councils, attorney-development staff and innovation leaders use the tool to pursue consistency, relevance and engagement in training. Large firms are the documented market, including Littler's labor-and-employment practice; the source does not establish comparable effects for smaller firms or public legal services. Firms potentially save on actors and off-site training, although neither realized savings nor consequences for those suppliers are reported. Clients are implicated by Larsen's observation that they may not want junior lawyers learning through live depositions, not by evidence of measured improvements in case outcomes. AltaClaro and Verbit supply training and transcription technology; the account does not describe them delivering client legal work as ALSPs. Planned expansion would reach lawyers undertaking trial advocacy, oral argument, interviews and negotiation. The source does not claim displacement of legal jobs, changes to staffing leverage or improved access to justice.
